newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Bel-20 Index to re-test 1,900 points.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Bel-20 Index to re-test 1,900 points.

text.p: Belgian shares took heart from a positive Wall Street on Monday, with the Bel-20 leading stock index ending at 1,898.76 points - a new record closing high.
But dealers were mixed on whether the index could make a clear break over 1,900 points, after it hit 1,906.38 in early trade only to fall back in later dealings.
"It will depend largely on what happens in America and with the dollar. Interest rates seem to be less important right now," said a trader at G-Securities.
The Bel-20 was spurred higher on Monday by the Dow Jones .DJI 101-point gain last Friday and the dollar's firm tone.
The Dow was again firm on Monday, up nearly 50 points at the Belgian market's close.
"If the Dow continues to perform well we will have no problem (breaking 1,900) tomorrow," said another trader.

The G-Securities trader noted, however, some hesitancy on the part of end-investors. "People have a lot of cash to invest but are asking themselves whether the time to buy is now or whether they should wait a bit for a correction."
Cyclical shares were most in demand on Monday, following a raft of buy recommendations on industrial stocks.
Cement maker CBR rose 3.38 pct to 3,060 francs.

Supermarket group Delhaize was up 2.38 pct at 1,935 francs after its U.S. Food Lion unit announced strong fourth quarter figures and in anticipation its own 1996 data, due for release on Friday, would be equally good.
Plastic window frame maker Deceuninck, long a market darling, closed up 150 francs, or 2.68 pct, at 5,750 francs, a new all-time high.

Steel maker Cockerill Sambre reversed recent weakness, which coincided with it being dropped from the Bel-20 Index, to rise eight francs, or 6.72 percent, to 127 francs. Dealers said the stock was helped by the demise of Clabecq.
Clabecq was declared bankrupt on Friday and the Brussels Stock Exchange's management committee said its share would be delisted this week.

Some traders also believed Clabecq hit bottom at the end of last year and are looking forward to 1998, when the company should pay off a large accumulated preferred dividend, one trader said. No dividend is expected on 1996 earnings.
Luxembourg steel group Arbed rose 40 francs, or 1.16 percent, to 3,490 francs.
